title: The Iran War Just Went Gulf-Wide. For Nine Million Indians in the Region, the Fight Is Now Overhead.
excerpt: Iranian missiles struck targets in five Gulf states in a single day. The U.S. hit 300 targets in three nights. The Strait of Hormuz is closed again. And India's largest overseas community is caught in the middle.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Iranian missiles struck five Gulf states, escalating the conflict significantly.
  • The U.S. military targeted over 300 Iranian sites in three nights.
  • The Strait of Hormuz is reportedly closed, impacting global oil supply.
  • Nine million Indians in the Gulf face immediate risks from the conflict.
  • India's economy may suffer from rising oil prices and inflation.

The war between the United States and Iran broke new boundaries over the weekend. For the first time since the conflict began in February, Iranian missiles struck targets across five Gulf states in a single day — Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman and the United Arab Emirates — while the U.S. military hit more than 300 Iranian military targets in three consecutive nights of bombardment. The escalation transformed what had been a narrowly contained fight over the Strait of Hormuz into the widest theatre of hostilities the Gulf has witnessed in decades. For the nine million Indians who live and work across these countries, the war is no longer something happening in the background. It is now overhead. ## How We Got Here The unravelling began on Tuesday, when Washington revoked a sanctions waiver that had briefly allowed limited Iranian crude sales. Three commercial tankers — Qatari and Saudi-flagged — had come under fire in the strait earlier in the week. In response, U.S. forces struck Iranian coastal and missile installations. Iran retaliated by targeting American military sites in Kuwait and Bahrain, as it had done intermittently since April. Then on Saturday, Iran went further. The Revolutionary Guards said they had destroyed a command-and-control centre and drone hangars at an American base in Jordan, struck a radar installation in Kuwait, attacked U.S. aircraft carrier support platforms in Oman, and destroyed a fighter jet maintenance facility and command centre in Qatar. The UAE said its air defence systems engaged Iranian missiles and drones. Warning sirens sounded in Bahrain. Explosions were heard in Doha. U.S. Central Command confirmed it struck approximately 140 Iranian military targets on Saturday alone — missile and drone sites, naval capabilities, ammunition depots, communications infrastructure and coastal surveillance positions. Across three nights, the total exceeded 300. ## Hormuz Shut Again > **"## Hormuz Shut Again Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed "until the end of U.S."** Iran declared the Strait of Hormuz closed "until the end of U.S. interference in this region," after firing what it called a warning shot at a commercial vessel travelling on an "unauthorised route." A second vessel was struck and disabled, the Guards said. U.S. Central Command disputed the closure, saying commercial ships continue to transit the waterway, but vessel-tracking data earlier in the week showed tanker crossings had collapsed to just seven per day — against a daily average of eighteen in the first week of July. The strait carries roughly one-fifth of the world's crude oil and a significant share of its liquefied natural gas. Brent crude climbed to $76 a barrel on Friday, up $4 from before the latest fighting, and analysts warned of sharper spikes if hostilities intensify. "If the peace deal breaks, it won't just raise oil prices; it would also increase pressure on AI supply chains in Asia, force central banks to be hawkish, tighten financial conditions, and could shift the outcome of the U.S. midterms," wrote Ryan Sweet, chief global economist at Oxford Economics. "The cascade runs fast." ## The New Supreme Leader Weighs In In a written statement released on Saturday to mark funeral ceremonies for his father, Iran's new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, pledged vengeance for the death of the elder Khamenei, who was killed in the opening phase of the war. "We pledge to avenge the blood of the martyred leader and all the martyrs," the statement said, adding that the vengeance would occur "whatever happened to Iran." The younger Khamenei has not appeared in public since the war began. His statement was the most direct signal yet that Iran's clerical leadership is not seeking de-escalation. Iran's top negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, posted on X: "The era of one-sided deals is OVER. We told you: keep your word or pay the price. Reality is knocking."

## What It Means for India India imports nearly 85 per cent of its crude oil. While its supply basket has diversified — with Russian, West African and Latin American grades reducing dependence on the Gulf — liquefied petroleum gas and natural gas remain far more exposed. LPG is the primary cooking fuel for over 335 million Indian households. A prolonged Hormuz closure would tighten availability, push up freight and insurance costs, and feed directly into consumer prices. Indian markets took their worst hit in over two months on Wednesday, with the Sensex falling 2.1 per cent and the Nifty 50 dropping 2 per cent after Trump declared the ceasefire "over." The rupee slipped to 95.55 per dollar, its weakest level in a month. ANZ expects India's retail inflation to rise to 4.3 per cent, with analysts warning of second-round effects if energy costs stay elevated. But the immediate human stakes are in the Gulf itself. An estimated 9 million Indians — the largest expatriate community in the region — work across the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman and Bahrain. Some 6,000 Indian seafarers are stranded in the Persian Gulf. India has already opened direct talks with Iran to secure passage for nine trapped tankers and nearly 200 sailors. New Delhi has also dispatched a naval detachment to the region. The Indian Foreign Ministry has urged citizens in affected areas to exercise caution and register with local embassies. For families in Kerala, Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Uttar Pradesh who depend on Gulf remittances — which totalled over $28 billion from the region last year — the question is no longer whether the war will reach them. It already has. ## What Comes Next Omani and Iranian diplomats met in Oman over the weekend to discuss "mechanisms for the safe passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz." Oman's state news agency said talks would continue at "technical and political levels."

But the gap between the two sides appears to be widening. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi has accused the United States of violating the ceasefire. Trump, who faces a politically sensitive gasoline-price environment ahead of November's congressional elections, has left the door open to negotiations even as the military campaign intensifies. For India, the calculus is shifting. The government had been quietly exploring a return to Iranian crude imports under the now-revoked sanctions waiver. That option is off the table for the foreseeable future. India's strategy, officials say, is to deepen alternative supply routes, protect its citizens abroad, and wait — hoping diplomacy catches up before the bills do.
